title: The Connection Between Culture and Thought
sourceHeading: The Connection Between Culture and Thought

source.filename: Practice 52  IETLS 閱讀練習 - Passage 1.pdf

paragraphs.label: A
paragraphs.text: The world’s population has surpassed 7 billion and continues to grow. Across the globe, humans have many differences. These differences can be influenced by factors such as geography, climate, politics, nationality and many others. Culture is one such aspect that can change the way people behave.

paragraphs.label: B
paragraphs.text: Your culture may influence your clothing, your language, and many aspects of your life. But is culture influential enough to change the way an individual thinks? It has long been believed that people from different cultures would think differently. For example, a young boy from a farm would talk about cows while a boy from New York would talk about cars. If two young children from different countries were asked what they thought about a painting, they would answer differently because of their cultural backgrounds.

paragraphs.label: C
paragraphs.text: In recent years, new research has challenged this long-held belief. This work is not the first, however, to explore the possibility that culture can change how we think; earlier studies provided valuable insight into the question. One of the earliest projects was carried out in the Soviet Union and sought to determine whether culture affected people’s ways of processing thoughts. The researchers focused on how living environment and nationality might influence cognition. Nisbett’s experiment investigated this aspect of cognitive psychology, and he conducted several versions to test different processes.

paragraphs.label: D
paragraphs.text: One experiment led by Nisbett and Masuda showed participants an animated video of a large fish swimming among smaller fish and other sea creatures, then asked them to describe the scene. Japanese participants tended to focus on the aquatic background, including plants and the colour of the water, as well as relationships between the large and small fish. American participants focused on individual fish, particularly the larger, more distinctive-looking one. The experiment suggested that members of Eastern cultures focus more on the overall picture, whereas those from Western cultures focus more on individuals.

paragraphs.label: E
paragraphs.text: In another experiment, performed by Nisbett and Choi, participants were presented with convincing evidence supporting a position. Both Korean and American groups initially expressed strong support. After receiving evidence opposing that position, Koreans began to modify or reduce their support, whereas Americans strengthened their support for the original argument. This suggested that in Korean culture, support for an argument depends more on context. Ideas and conclusions are flexible, so individuals may be more willing to change their minds. Americans, by contrast, were less willing to alter their original conclusion.

paragraphs.label: F
paragraphs.text: Nisbett and Ara devised an experiment to test thought processing in Eastern and Western cultures. Participants were given the argument: ‘All animals with fur hibernate. Rabbits have fur. Therefore, rabbits hibernate.’ People from Eastern cultures questioned the conclusion because they knew that some furry animals do not hibernate. American participants, however, considered the statement correct. They assumed that if the logical deduction was based on a correct premise, the conclusion must also be right.

paragraphs.label: G
paragraphs.text: These early experiments might seem to confirm the original premise that culture affects how we think. Recent researchers, however, have criticised both that view and Nisbett’s experiments. Although the studies challenged earlier beliefs about thought processing, the extent to which other factors shaped the results required further discussion. Fischer considers Nisbett’s work valuable because it provides qualitative descriptions, although not results from a controlled environment. Chang partly agrees, noting that social factors might also influence the findings.

paragraphs.label: H
paragraphs.text: Another criticism of Nisbett’s experiments is that culture was studied as a sub-factor of nationality. The experiments assumed that culture would be the same among all members of a nationality. For example, every American who participated in the experiments could be assumed to have the same culture. In reality, culture is much more complicated than nationality. These early experiments did not control for other factors, such as socioeconomic status, education, ethnicity, and regional differences in culture. All of these factors could have a big effect on the individual’s response.

paragraphs.label: I
paragraphs.text: A third criticism of Nisbett’s experiment is that the content itself should have been more abstract, such as a puzzle or an IQ test. With objective content, such as nature and animals, people from different countries of the world might have different preconceived ideas about these animals. Prior knowledge based on geographic location would further complicate the results. A test that is more abstract, or more quantitative, would provide a more controlled study of how cognitive processing works for different groups of people.

paragraphs.label: J
paragraphs.text: The research on culture’s effect on cognitive processing still goes on today, and while some criticisms exist of Nisbett’s early studies, the projects still provide valuable insight. It is important for future research projects to control carefully for variables such as culture. Something like culture is complex and difficult to define. It can also be influenced by many other variables, such as geography or education styles. When studying a variable like culture, it is critical that the researcher create a clear definition for what is—and what is not—considered culture.

paragraphs.label: K
paragraphs.text: Another important consideration in modern research is ethics. Researchers must consider carefully whether their findings could harm any group involved. In an increasingly globalised employment market, generalisations about nationalities can damage prospective employees. Such information might also affect the design of tests and university-admissions standards, potentially favouring one group or disadvantaging another. When studying culture and nationality, researchers should consider every positive and negative effect their published conclusions may have.
